body:
## What

Incremental evaluation's reuse check (`IncrEval.reuse_check`) recognizes an unchanged expression by its Merkle hash, and remembers each comparison it makes. It no longer walks the subterm again for every check.

### The cost before

The check compares each node's cached elaboration with the new one, structurally, with `Exp.fast_equal`. Statics builds fresh objects on every run, so physical equality never helps, and every check walked its whole subterm.

An edit near the end of a program sits inside every enclosing `let`. So the checks along that spine walk down to the edit each time, which is O(n²) in all.

### The change

- **`Util.ValueHash`** (new): hashes any immutable value by its runtime structure, ids included, and keeps each object's hash in a JS `WeakMap`. `ValueHash.Pairs` remembers an answer per pair of objects.
  - A value it can't hash soundly (a function, an unforced lazy, a cycle) has no hash, and `same` answers false, so callers compare as before.
- **`Equality.equality(~hash_shortcut=true, …)`**: two subterms with the same hash are equal without a walk, and the answer for a pair of subterms is remembered.
  - It applies only under identity renamings, and only when the settings carry no environments and no free-variable handler. Otherwise identical terms need not be equal.
  - Without alpha-equivalence, renamings only ever pair a name with itself, so that condition costs nothing for syntactic settings.
- **`Exp.fast_equal_hashed`**: `fast_equal` with the shortcut.
- **`reuse_check`**: first asks whether the whole elaboration is the same build (`ValueHash.same`), then compares structure and lexemes in one memoized walk (`fast_equal_hashed_with_lexemes`, below).

Every other caller of `Equality` behaves as before; the shortcut is off by default.

## Measured

Node, `dev`'s test build. The program is 400 definitions of the form `let fi = fun x -> if x < i then (x + i, [x, x * 2, x * 3], "si") else (x - 1, [x], "t") in`, then a tuple applying each one.

Each run evaluates the program, edits the final literal while keeping every id (as the editor does), runs statics, then times only the incremental re-evaluation. Seven runs each:

| | re-evaluation, ms | median |
|---|---|---|
| before | 2743 4221 2746 2436 2418 3099 2719 | 2743 |
| hashing only (no pair memo) | 4276 3998 4219 4650 4446 4353 4438 | 4353 |
| this PR | 502 375 363 367 416 410 421 | 410 |

Hashing alone was slower on this program. Every check along the `let` spine still walked down to the edit, now paying for the hashing too. Remembering the answer per pair is what makes each check after the first one a lookup.

The benchmark isn't committed: one run takes over a minute.

### Lexemes in the same walk (second commit)

The check also compared the two sides' lexemes, so that an in-place edit of an unknown operator (`@@` to `@@@`) invalidates reuse. It did that by building a lexeme trace of each whole subterm, which neither the hash nor the memo covers. When a subterm comes back with new ids and nothing else changed, every enclosing `let` fails the hash, and each one traces its whole body: quadratic again.

- **`Equality.equality(~lexemes=true, …)`**: every walker (expressions, patterns, types, type patterns, rules, modules, signatures, module patterns) also requires the two nodes' lexemes to be equal, inside the same hash shortcut and memo.
- **`Exp.fast_equal_hashed_with_lexemes`** uses it, and `reuse_check` calls it in place of `fast_equal_hashed` followed by the two traces.

Node, `dev`'s test build: a chain of n `let`s compared with a copy of itself under new ids (`Exp.replace_all_ids`), once for every enclosing `let`, as the check asks about them. Two runs each:

| n | before, ms | after, ms |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 72, 77 | 1, 1 |
| 200 | 300, 309 | 1, 2 |
| 400 | 1,323, 1,297 | 4, 4 |

On the livelits branch (hazelgrove/hazel#2635), opening a livelit's picture as its own cell makes it elaborate again, with new ids, on every change. There, 122 enclosing `let`s took 1.45–2.5 s of the worker per slider change; after, 1–4 ms, with the same reuse decisions, and the change went from 3.5 s to 1.26 s. Details: [Hazel reports, issue 008](http://matthewhammer.org/hazel/reports/008/).

On the livelits branch, this check was ~280 ms of the eval worker's ~410 ms per slider release in Firefox. Details are in hazelgrove/hazel#2609 and [Hazel reports, issue 001](http://matthewhammer.org/hazel/reports/001/).

## Tests

- New `ValueHash` group:
  - a copy (made by `Marshal`, as a request is) hashes the same as the original;
  - different values, or the same text elaborated twice with fresh ids, do not;
  - a closure never compares the same;
  - `fast_equal_hashed` agrees with `fast_equal` on a copy and on an edit, including when asked a second time (from memory);
  - `Pairs` remembers an answer only for exactly that pair.
- New in `Evaluator.Incremental`: the one-walk check agrees with the trace check (the same term under new ids: equal; a lexeme-only edit: not; a real change: not). The existing "lexeme-only edit invalidates reuse" still passes.
- The quick suite (4,323 tests) passed with the first commit. With the second: `Evaluator.Incremental` (42), `Evaluator` (493), `Equality` (6) and `ValueHash` (5) pass.

commits.messageBody:
IncrEval.reuse_check proves a node unchanged by its Merkle hash, or
else by fast_equal_hashed (memoized across checks) and a lexeme trace
of each side. The traces were not memoized: when a subterm comes back
with new ids and nothing else changed, every enclosing let that holds
it fails the hash, and each builds traces of its whole body, so the
check is quadratic in the depth of the let chain.

Equality takes ~lexemes: each walker (exp, pat, typ, tpat, rul, mod,
sig, mpat) also requires equal lexemes, inside the same hash shortcut
and memo. Exp.fast_equal_hashed_with_lexemes uses it, and the reuse
check calls it instead of fast_equal_hashed && trace == trace.

Measured here, comparing a chain of n lets with a copy of it under
new ids (Exp.replace_all_ids), every enclosing let as the reuse check
asks about it, two runs: n = 100, 200, 400 took 72-77, 300-309 and
1,297-1,323 ms before, and 1, 1-2 and 4 ms after.

Measured on #2635 (the Livelit Playground's Full Body slide, UX mode
with the picture's cell open, which elaborates the cell again with
new ids on every change): 122 such lets per slider change took
1.45-2.5 s; after, 1-4 ms with identical reuse decisions, and the
change from release to redraw went from 3.5 s to 1.26 s (median of 12).
Performance analysis issue 008.

Tests: a new one, the one-walk check agrees with the trace check (new
ids: equal; a lexeme-only edit: not; a real change: not). The
existing "lexeme-only edit invalidates reuse" passes.
Evaluator.Incremental 42, Evaluator 493, Equality 6, ValueHash 5.

(cherry picked from commit cbdab791f5, adapted to this branch)
